{"id": "39:10/q12", "question": "What does أَرْضٌ mean in Arabic usage?", "turns_on": "Whether the question concerns the ordinary root sense or its particular Qur'anic geographical uses.", "positions": [{"id": "39:10/q12/p1", "position": "Earth is named for breadth; related expressions extend the root to expansiveness.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī calls earth the familiar broad expanse. Ibn al-Sikkīt says a sore “arḍ” when it spreads; Ibn Fāris says any broad thing is arḍ and arīḍ describes a man suited to good. The same lexicon records termite-eaten wood, a wool or hair carpet, approaching someone, a foreigner, lush land, and Ibn ʿAbbās's distinction between earth's and one's own trembling."}, {"id": "39:10/q12/p2", "position": "Across Qur'anic passages, arḍ can denote Paradise, Mecca, Medina, or Syria.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī cites Paradise at 21:105 and 39:74, Mecca at 4:97 and 13:41, Medina at 4:97, 4:100, 17:76 and 29:56, and Syria at 7:137 and 21:71; he includes 39:10 among Medina examples."}]}
{"id": "39:10/q13", "question": "What does “God's earth is vast” refer to here?", "turns_on": "Whether the land is a worldly destination, the Garden, provision from the earth, or inward spiritual space.", "positions": [{"id": "39:10/q13/p1", "position": "The broad worldly earth offers other places where believers can worship safely.", "reasons": "Mujāhid explains leaving idol worship; al-Ṭabarī says leave polytheist territory; Ibn ʿAbbās ties it to leaving Mecca and 4:97; al-Rāzī and al-Nasafī cite prophets and the righteous as precedents. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says nearby lands fit the migration story; al-Rāzī and Ālūsī prefer this because subsequent patience fits migration. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the obvious fact an indirect exhortation like a proverb, with 4:97 explicit. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī takes the historically Meccan pressure as particular but wording general."}, {"id": "39:10/q13/p2", "position": "It is Paradise or the broad Garden sought through righteous deeds.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās reports the Garden; al-Thaʿlabī reports Muqātil; Ibn ʿĪsā, Abū Muslim and al-Ṭabrisī offer it to encourage goodness. Abū Muslim cites 39:74 and 3:133 and the movement from piety to Paradise. Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls it unsupported, al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī remote, and Kuranyolu weak."}, {"id": "39:10/q13/p3", "position": "It designates Medina, the destination of migration.", "reasons": "Muqātil identifies Medina; ʿAṭāʾ likewise calls it the migration land or Medina, with relief from enemies as the good; Ibn al-Jawzī cites this verse among Medina uses."}, {"id": "39:10/q13/p4", "position": "Its breadth signals abundant provision or fruitful lands available to believers.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī prefers this because the clause presents a favor; al-Jishumī reports fruitful lands; al-Qurṭubī finds provision plausible and recalls Sufyān al-Thawrī's advice to move to cheaper bread."}, {"id": "39:10/q13/p5", "position": "Inwardly it is the expanded self or heart, or limitless divine presence.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī describes the contented self freed by certainty; al-Baqlī says the Real expands the heart. {"id": "39:10/q14", "question": "What practical migration does the spacious earth call for?", "turns_on": "Whether migration is the concrete response to persecution, a move for provision, or a broader departure from conditions that impede goodness.", "positions": [{"id": "39:10/q14/p1", "position": "Leave a place where religion cannot be practiced or sin is forced or openly practiced.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj cites 4:97 for leaving idol pressure; al-Naḥḥās and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr extend flight to sinful settings. Al-Qushayrī and later exegetes say persecution cannot excuse abandoning worship. Bursawī cites a report promising Paradise for migration to protect faith and distinguishes that motive from worldly moves to a more sinful place. Iṣlāḥī says move if Makkah makes worship impossible."}, {"id": "39:10/q14/p2", "position": "Migration may include moving to land with cheaper living or better provision.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī draws this from al-Māwardī's provision reading and quotes Sufyān al-Thawrī on cheaper bread."}, {"id": "39:10/q14/p3", "position": "The enduring sense includes spiritual migration from evil and changes in work or place.", "reasons": "Asad sees the capacity always to do good and cites 4:97; Kuranyolu ranges from changing jobs to changing countries when one cannot live one's values or improve conditions."}]}
{"id": "39:10/q15", "question": "What migration setting lies behind the verse?", "turns_on": "Whether the historical allusion concerns the first migration to Abyssinia or departure toward Medina.", "positions": [{"id": "39:10/q15/p1", "position": "It alludes to Jaʿfar and companions' migration to Abyssinia.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya report the group preparing or enduring trials and emigrating; al-Qurṭubī and Ibn ʿĀshūr attribute the identification to Ibn ʿAbbās. Abū Ḥayyān and Ālūsī repeat it. Ibn ʿĀshūr dates the Abyssinian move to year five before the later Medinan migration, with 83 men and 19 women excluding children, under a just king; he also recounts Abū Bakr's interrupted attempted departure and says the Prophet remained to establish Islam in Mecca until Medina was ready."}, {"id": "39:10/q15/p2", "position": "It urges leaving Mecca for Medina or another safe land.", "reasons": "Muqātil names Medina; Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Rāzī make Mecca the point of departure. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the reassurance eases leaving home and 4:97 makes migration explicit; Iṣlāḥī describes Quraysh pressure and a land that would receive expelled Muslims."}]}
{"id": "39:10/q16", "question": "How is the spacious-earth clause linked to the promise around it?", "turns_on": "Whether the aside addresses practical worship and migration or climate and bodily welfare.", "positions": [{"id": "39:10/q16/p1", "position": "It removes the excuse that homeland prevents excellence and prepares the special reward for patient migrants.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī calls it an aside and argues the next clause distinguishes migrants, whose sacrifices follow prophets and righteous people; he prefers this to a climate-and-health connection, citing 4:97 and 29:56 and the nearer attachment rule. Al-Biqāʿī says all land lies under God's power. Ibn ʿĀshūr sees an indirect call that consoles those leaving home."}, {"id": "39:10/q16/p2", "position": "It meets concerns about climate and bodily health while contrasting immediate worldly good with later full reward.", "reasons": "Al-Kashf calls this explanatory connection finer than a restrictive circumstantial parse; Ālūsī acknowledges its merit but prefers the obedience-and-migration connection."}]}
{"id": "39:10/q17", "question": "Who are ٱلصَّٰبِرُونَ here?", "turns_on": "Whether patience is specified by migration, affliction, obedience, fasting, or inward discipline.", "positions": [{"id": "39:10/q17/p1", "position": "They endure persecution, migration, exile from home and kin, and hardship for religion.", "reasons": "Muqātil connects patience to emigration. Al-Baghawī mentions steadfast faith and Jaʿfar's companions; Ibn ʿAṭiyya includes hardship, emigration and aid to faith. Al-Rāzī, al-Nasafī, al-Biqāʿī, Bursawī, Ālūsī, Ibn ʿĀshūr and Iṣlāḥī emphasize the cost of leaving home. Kuranyolu points to sacrifice for values and 4:97–100."}, {"id": "39:10/q17/p2", "position": "They endure all afflictions and trials with composure.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī takes life's ordeals generally; al-Zajjāj links hardship to obedience; Qushayrī describes restraining the self and accepting decree without protest. Al-Qurṭubī cites Mālik on calamities and griefs; Ibn ʿĀshūr defines composure when pain arrives. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī and Ālūsī say the wording is unrestricted despite migration's context."}, {"id": "39:10/q17/p3", "position": "They persevere in obedience, duties, and avoidance of sin.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās says ṣābir praises restraint from sin and distinguishes patience “with” sin from patience “on” misfortune. Junayd adds restraining limbs while seeking reward; Ṭāhir al-Maqdisī distinguishes patience from, for, upon and in God, calling obedience easiest. Ibn ʿĀshūr includes commands and prohibitions, with reward varying by degree."}, {"id": "39:10/q17/p4", "position": "They are those tested with illness and worldly calamity.", "reasons": "Reports from Anas and others identify the afflicted whose reward surpasses ordinary deeds; al-Qurṭubī's Mālik includes grief and trial."}, {"id": "39:10/q17/p5", "position": "Inwardly they bear affliction, restrain the self, and steadily advance through unveiled states.", "reasons": "Al-Muḥāsibī's arrows of affliction occur in al-Sulamī and Bursawī; Junayd speaks of carrying hardship to its end. Al-Khawwāṣ criticizes reliance on worldly means and Dhū al-Nūn's poem depicts love's tears. Yūsuf ibn al-Ḥusayn asks for delight and contentment rather than aversion; al-Qāshānī and al-Baqlī speak of effacement and concealed unveiling."}, {"id": "39:10/q17/p6", "position": "They are those who fast.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī reports this from the divine saying that fasting belongs to God, with its reward uniquely His; other scholars say other deeds are weighed while fasting is rewarded in handfuls."}]}

{"id": "39:10/q19", "question": "How does the closing promise work grammatically and rhetorically?", "turns_on": "Whether the circumstantial phrase describes the reward or its recipients.", "positions": [{"id": "39:10/q19/p1", "position": "بغير حساب is circumstantial for the reward, expressing uncountable abundance.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn permits the reward attachment; al-Nasafī says it describes the reward circumstantially. Al-Sāmarrāʾī reports commentators attaching 'without reckoning' to the reward, indicating reward poured out abundantly."}, {"id": "39:10/q19/p2", "position": "بغير حساب is circumstantial for the patient, who are not called to account.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn permits the people attachment; Ālūsī calls it less immediate. {"id": "39:10/q21", "question": "Which reports illustrate the special reward for afflicted patient people?", "turns_on": "Whether reports distinguish the afflicted by absence of scale, absence of record, particular acts of patience, or general trial.", "positions": [{"id": "39:10/q21/p1", "position": "Afflicted people receive poured-out reward without a scale or record, making the spared envy them.", "reasons": "Anas reports contrast measured worship with limitless affliction reward; al-Ṭabrisī says no scale or register when balances appear. Al-Durr adds a report that God may intensify trials of a beloved servant while hearing supplication, then grant, store or avert harm."}, {"id": "39:10/q21/p2", "position": "The afflicted receive unmeasured reward beneath a tree of tribulation in Paradise.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī recounts Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī's report of obligations, contentment and the tree; al-Qurṭubī attributes a version to al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī from his grandfather and says it concludes by reciting this verse; al-Durr records a tree and no register or scale."}, {"id": "39:10/q21/p3", "position": "Further Prophetic counsel commends endurance and ties greater trials to greater rank.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī reports advice to endure harm and a warning through Abū Dharr that impatience leads toward Hell, citing 13:24. {"id": "39:10/q27", "question": "What accompanying source excerpts discuss literary comparison rather than directly explaining 39:10?", "turns_on": "The cited passages themselves concern different poetic and rhetorical material.", "positions": [{"id": "39:10/q27/p1", "position": "Al-Bāqillānī criticizes a poem's weak joins, familiar wordplay, diction, forced rhyme, and uneven imagery.", "reasons": "He finds an opening disconnected and derivative, the distance line pleasing but commonplace, the stellar reins objectionable, two panegyric lines alien, tribal names stylistically clumsy despite a sound threat, and genealogical rhyme forced; he contrasts a stronger Banu Tamīm line."}, {"id": "39:10/q27/p2", "position": "Al-Jurjānī surveys rational and conventional similes, including figurative spaciousness.", "reasons": "In Asrār he compares night and pilgrim stars, moon emerging from clouds as relief, clear light interrupted by darkness as joy and grief, fire and coal as justice and injustice, a generous person's wide character as a road, and the breadth of hope against a barren plain; he introduces another darkness comparison. The width examples illustrate why a moral metaphor can feel sensory."}, {"id": "39:10/q27/p3", "position": "Al-Jurjānī argues rhetorical composition is the ordered relation of meanings.", "reasons": "In Dalāʾil he reasons that verbal sequence alone cannot explain unequal judgments of quality; thought must work on the craft's object, and word order follows meanings already ordered in the mind."}]}
{"id": "39:10/q28", "question": "What other adjacent lexical or exegetical extracts appear in the notes?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:10/q28/p1", "position": "A destination may be described as a place judged by God alone.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī reports Abū ʿAlī's comparison with a matter referred to a prince; this excerpt is from a different part of his commentary."}, {"id": "39:10/q28/p2", "position": "Mabwaʾ denotes a settled, secure and suitable dwelling or station.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ cites al-Harawī's definition and applies the root to the Prophet's placing believers in defensible battle stations, mentioning 59:9, 39:74 and 3:121."}, {"id": "39:10/q28/p3", "position": "A separate report says only sincere religion is accepted.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī transmits the Prophet's answer that ostentatious charity earns no reward and connects it to 39:3."}, {"id": "39:10/q28/p4", "position": "Gratitude should recur more often than patience.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī reasons that blessings persist moment by moment, while patience arises in particular acts or hardships."}]}
{"id": "39:10/q29", "question": "Why does 39:10 state that God's earth is vast with less emphasis than 29:56?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:10/q29/p1", "position": "The emphasis supplied by possessives and inna in 29:56 is unnecessary in 39:10.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī observes that 29:56 reinforces the servants' and earth's relation to God with possessives and inna, while 39:10 gives the spacious-earth statement without that extra emphasis."}]}
{"id": "39:15/q01", "question": "What occasion and audience prompted the challenge to worship as they wished?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:15/q01/p1", "position": "It addresses the polytheists who urged Muhammad to abandon his religion and follow his forefathers' faith.", "reasons": "Jishumi reports an invitation to follow the ancestors; Nasafi says they called him a loser for leaving them; Bursevi records the taunt; Ibn Ashur cites Muqatil's report that Quraysh asked why he adopted this religion and urged the faith of their fathers and leaders, and identifies the two parties from context."}]}
{"id": "39:15/q02", "question": "How does the opening challenge follow the Prophet's declaration of exclusive worship?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:15/q02/p1", "position": "His exclusive devotion and disavowal of partners lead to a direct challenge to the polytheists, followed by an indirect warning about their loss.", "reasons": "Tabari says the Prophet declares sincere undivided obedience to God alone and renounces rivals. {"id": "39:15/q03", "question": "What force does the command to worship whatever they wish have?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:15/q03/p1", "position": "It is a threatening rebuke that leaves persistent idolaters to their choice and its punishment, while disavowing their worship.", "reasons": "Tabari says they may choose created objects but will learn the result before their Lord. Zajjaj compares the command to enjoying disbelief briefly (18:29); Thalabi, Ibn Atiyya, Qurtubi, Bursevi, and Abu Hayyan compare 41:40 or 39:8. Kashshaf and Abu Hayyan stress abandonment; Razi says the case for monotheism is complete, so this is no genuine command. Ibn Jawzi says it is a threat, not an operative command. Qushayri calls it the utmost threat; Baydawi, Ibn Kathir, and Study Quran pair threat with repudiation, the latter citing 6:19, 6:78, 10:41, and 109:6. Biqai says nothing below God can provide His favor. Bursevi, al-Irshad, and Alusi hear anger at persistence after prohibition, inviting punishment. Ibn Ashur hears an indifferent leave-taking grounded in whim, paralleling 18:29. Tabatabai says the choice will not benefit them. Islahi says the Prophet's public disavowal withstands coercion and oppression. Qurtubi calls it warning and rebuke."}]}
{"id": "39:15/q04", "question": "What is the relation of this command to the later command to fight?", "turns_on": "Whether a threatening, nonoperative imperative is susceptible to abrogation; Zajjaj supplies only chronology.", "positions": [{"id": "39:15/q04/p1", "position": "The fighting verse abrogated this command.", "reasons": "Thalabi and Qurtubi report this as another view."}, {"id": "39:15/q04/p2", "position": "It cannot be abrogated because it is a threat rather than an operative command.", "reasons": "Ibn Jawzi expressly rejects abrogation on this ground."}, {"id": "39:15/q04/p3", "position": "Its threatening wording indicates that it preceded the command to fight.", "reasons": "Zajjaj infers this chronology from the threat and compares 18:29; he does not state that fighting abrogated it."}]}

{"id": "39:15/q08", "question": "How do the losers lose themselves?", "turns_on": "The notes variously locate self-loss in punishment, in the unbelieving choices that waste one's capacities, or in the combined loss of worldly and future good.", "positions": [{"id": "39:15/q08/p1", "position": "They perish or suffer lasting punishment in Hell, shut out from Paradise and reunion.", "reasons": "Muqatil relates punishment to failure to affirm God's oneness. Tabari says they perish under God's punishment; Ibn Abbas adds lost worldly life and barred Paradise (22:11), Ibn Zayd says loss starts in this world, and Mujahid says they die while still alive in the Fire. Zajjaj, Wahidi, and Razi specify everlasting Hell; Mawardi and Bagawi give entry into Hell; Ibn Kathir and Abu Hayyan stress separation. Durr reports Mujahid's conscious regret; Bursevi and Alusi specify everlasting exposure; Kuranyolu says the punishment is deserved. Asad describes destruction of true human identity and uniqueness; Study Quran says the chance for good and repentance has been squandered (22:11)."}, {"id": "39:15/q08/p2", "position": "By choosing unbelief and misguidance they squander their God-given capacities, deeds, and possibility of happiness.", "reasons": "Bursevi and Kashifi describe ruin or straying within oneself. Baydawi and Nasafi say they misguide or destroy themselves. Razi compares reason and good deeds to capital: first principles yield acquired knowledge, life and ability should yield good works, but disbelievers expend intellect and strength on delusion and evil, lose everything at death, and incur punishment. Alusi says they squander what they needed to secure. Ibn Ashur says they cause punishment while imagining they secure bliss, like a trader (7:9). Tabatabai says unbelief destroys their capacity for happiness; Islahi warns against sacrificing the afterlife for brief pleasure."}, {"id": "39:15/q08/p3", "position": "They forfeit both this world and the afterlife, with the final deprivation worse than any worldly loss.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas in Tabari and Durr says they lose worldly life and Paradise. Study Quran ties the two losses to missed good deeds and repentance (22:11). Qushayri says desire loses the world and disobedience the afterlife; the Najmi interpretations reported by Bursevi add loss of the Lord through allegiance to another. Islahi calls worldly pleasures brief against eternal ruin."}]}

{"id": "39:15/q14", "question": "Why is this called 'the manifest loss'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:15/q14/p1", "position": "The independent, emphatic conclusion singles out this immense, unmistakable loss as the loss beside which others are negligible.", "reasons": "Kashshaf and Baydawi list the alerting particle, independent or resumed sentence, separating pronoun, definite noun, and 'manifest.' {"id": "39:15/q15", "question": "What makes this loss greater than ordinary worldly loss?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:15/q15/p1", "position": "It trades irreplaceable, lasting life and Paradise for Fire, whereas worldly goods and rank can be replaced or end soon.", "reasons": "Razi calls life, intellect, and ability God's capital for acquiring knowledge, good deeds, and afterlife; misuse wastes the investment and can turn exertion into punishment.
